chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Basir who said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) narrated to me that

his father — there was in his presence a woman from the Kharijites, I believe he said from the Clan of Hanifa. So a slave of his said to him: 'O son of the Messenger of God! In your presence is a woman who disavows your grandfather.' So it was decided for my father that he divorce her.
Then she claimed her dower against him, and brought him before the Emir of Medina seeking his aid. So the Emir of Medina said to him: 'O Ali! Either you swear an oath, or you give her her right.'

So he said to me: 'Arise, my son, and give her four hundred dinars.' So I said to him: 'O Father! May I be sacrificed for you! Are you not in the right?' He said: 'Yes, my son. But I held God in too high esteem to swear by Him a forced oath.'

key_terms.أجللت الله: I revered/held God too great — expression of deep taqwa-based reasoning; choosing to honor God's sanctity over legal entitlement
key_terms.الخوارج: The Kharijites — early sectarian faction who rejected the authority of Ali ibn Abi Talib (AS) and his descendants; their disavowal of the Prophet (SAWW) through his lineage is the theological provocation referenced here
key_terms.صداق: The mahr/dower — the obligatory gift from husband to wife stipulated in marriage, which the wife retains upon divorce
key_terms.يمين صبر: A forced or constrained oath (yamin sabr) — an oath sworn under legal compulsion, such as when a judge orders it; considered particularly serious in Islamic law

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Zayn al-Abidin pay his ex-wife's dowry instead of swearing an oath?
ai.summary: Imam Muhammad al-Baqir (peace be upon him) narrates that his father, Imam Zayn al-Abidin (Ali ibn al-Husayn), divorced a Kharijite wife and was brought before the governor of Medina when she demanded her mahr. Rather than swear an oath he was legally entitled to swear, the Imam chose to pay four hundred dinars, explaining to his son that he revered God too greatly to take a constrained (yamin sabr) oath. This account illustrates the Imam's profound reverence for the divine name and his willingness to bear financial loss rather than invoke God's name under legal compulsion — a principle that distinguishes genuine piety from mere legal compliance in Shia jurisprudential tradition.
